PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 71 — Lesson 95: Chronic Kidney Disease Management

FNP-level goal: Identify CKD accurately, distinguish chronic disease from acute change, reduce kidney and cardiovascular risk, use medication safely, monitor complications, and recognize when urgent or nephrology care is needed.

Learning Objectives

  • Use eGFR and albuminuria with time course to frame CKD risk.
  • Distinguish stable CKD from possible AKI or rapidly progressive disease.
  • Address BP, diabetes, cardiovascular risk, nephrotoxins, medication dosing, and volume/electrolyte safety.
  • Monitor anemia, mineral/bone, acid-base, potassium, and progression concerns when clinically indicated.
  • Recognize referral and emergency patterns.

Part 1 — CKD Is More Than a Creatinine

CKD involves persistent kidney damage and/or reduced kidney function over time. Interpret eGFR trend, albuminuria when indicated, urinalysis, BP, diabetes, medications, prior baseline, and clinical context. Creatinine alone can mislead because muscle mass and acute illness affect it. A sudden change from baseline, oliguria, dehydration, infection, obstruction symptoms, or new nephrotoxin exposure raises concern for AKI and requires a different pathway.

Part 2 — Risk Reduction Is Kidney and Cardiovascular Care

Manage BP, diabetes, tobacco exposure, lipid/CV risk, volume status, and medication safety using current guidelines. Review NSAIDs, contrast exposure, OTC products, supplements, diuretics, RAAS-active therapies, and other renally cleared or potassium-raising medicines. Do not stop or start important therapy reflexively; assess indication, current physiology, laboratory values, illness, and monitoring plan.

Part 3 — Albuminuria and Monitoring

Albuminuria can signal kidney injury and cardiovascular risk. Use appropriate repeat testing and context rather than treating one result as a final diagnosis. Monitor trends in renal function, electrolytes, BP, and diabetes risk. The right interval depends on stage, albuminuria, trajectory, treatment, and intercurrent illness. Assign ownership for results and patient communication.

Part 4 — Complications and Safety

Progressive CKD can contribute to hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia, volume overload, mineral/bone abnormalities, and medication toxicity. Ask about weakness, palpitations, dyspnea, edema, reduced urine, confusion, GI symptoms, and bleeding risk as clinically relevant. Severe hyperkalemia symptoms/ECG concern, pulmonary edema, uremic symptoms, rapidly worsening renal function, or suspected obstruction may require emergency evaluation.

Part 5 — Referral and Longitudinal Plan

Refer or seek nephrology input for advanced disease, rapid progression, difficult electrolyte/acid-base/volume issues, significant albuminuria or hematuria patterns, uncertain etiology, resistant hypertension, or preparation needs according to current guidance. Include baseline/trend data, medications, urine findings, comorbidities, imaging if available, and the specific question. Explain kidney-protection goals, sick-day/illness instructions when appropriate, and exact follow-up/return precautions.

Clinical Case

A 69-year-old with diabetes and heart failure has CKD, new diarrhea, reduced intake, NSAID use, rising creatinine, and potassium elevation.

FNP reasoning: assess for AKI and electrolyte danger, current volume status, medication exposures, symptoms, ECG/emergency need when indicated, and appropriate urgent evaluation. Do not frame this as routine CKD follow-up; acute physiology may be changing.

FNP CKD Framework

  1. Establish chronicity: baseline, trend, eGFR, urine/albumin context, and cause clues.
  2. Identify acute danger: AKI, obstruction, severe electrolyte/volume/uremic symptoms.
  3. Reduce risk: BP, diabetes, CV risk, nephrotoxins, and medication dosing/monitoring.
  4. Monitor complications: renal trend, potassium, acid-base, anemia, volume, and bone/mineral issues as appropriate.
  5. Coordinate: referral, result ownership, patient education, and safe follow-up.

High-Yield Summary

CKD: requires trend and damage context, not creatinine alone.
AKI concern: sudden change, illness, low intake, obstruction, or nephrotoxin exposure changes urgency.
Medication safety: review renal dosing, NSAIDs, potassium risk, and monitoring.
FNP standard: protect kidneys and cardiovascular health while recognizing acute danger and closing follow-up loops.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. CKD staging, medication changes, monitoring intervals, referral, dialysis planning, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, policy, scope, and the individual patient’s presentation.
